Murielle, the Sydney team wants the story behind our HR numbers. How did things use to work here?
Back then, we used to do everything on paper. The paperwork never ended, and payroll used to take three full days.
And turnover? I hear it used to be high.
Yes, it used to be eighteen percent. Nowadays, it is around nine percent.
That's a great story. At my old company, turnover used to be high too, mostly because of the long commute.
That was our problem too. We didn't use to have a hybrid schedule, and the hierarchy was very rigid.
So what changed? Did the company use to resist new technology?
A little. But in 2019 we digitized all employee records, and an app replaced the paper timesheets. Our HR has really evolved, and the old process looks outdated now.

Hi Murielle, it's Daniel from the Sydney office again. Thanks for the call last week. You asked me how our HR team used to work before the merger, so here is a quick answer. Ten years ago, we used to have four separate offices, and each office used to run its own payroll. Managers didn't use to share data, so nobody had the full picture. Recruitment used to take about three months. Nowadays, we have one HR system for the whole country, and we hire in about five weeks. People used to complain about the paperwork, but now most of it is digital. One thing hasn't changed: we still meet face to face every Friday morning. Speak soon.

When I started my career in HR, performance reviews used to happen once a year. Managers used to fill in a long form, and employees used to wait twelve months for any feedback. Most people hated it. Nowadays, many companies use short check-ins every month instead. Managers didn't use to talk about wellbeing, but today it is part of almost every conversation. Some things should stay the same, though. Good managers always listened carefully, and that is still the most important skill. So my advice is simple: keep what worked, and replace what is outdated.
